sources.title: Giulio Lucarini, Youssef Bokbot and Cyprian Broodbank, New Light on the Silent Millennia (2021)
sources.note: Original archaeological synthesis, published online 2020 and in African Archaeological Review 38 (2021), pp. 147 to 164; direct PDF read. Distinguish multiple economic traditions and caution about thin historical evidence. Recent Kach Kouch and Oued Beht findings update its evidence base.

sources.title: Ramzi Rouighi, The Andalusi origins of the Berbers? (2010)
sources.note: Primary historiographical argument; publisher abstract checked. Its particular proposed Andalusi origin is debated and is not asserted as fact. Used only to explain that applying one broad later name to ancient populations requires caution.

sources.title: Cyprian Broodbank and colleagues, Oued Beht, Morocco (2024)
sources.note: Primary 2021 to 2022 excavation report, Antiquity 98, pp. 1199 to 1218. Direct full PDF read. Oued Beht dates approximately 3400 to 2900 BCE, earlier background rather than part of the imported 1500 to 500 BCE interval. Excavators keep social organization and storage interpretation open; no language is assigned.

sources.title: Hamza Benattia and colleagues, Rethinking late prehistoric Mediterranean Africa: Kach Kouch (2025)
sources.note: Primary excavation report, Antiquity 99, pp. 354 to 374; full article directly read. KK2 approximately 1300 to 900 BCE, KK3 eighth to seventh centuries BCE. Stable settlement until approximately 600 BCE; no local language or named ancient ethnicity securely identified.

sources.title: Marta Portillo and colleagues, Domestic patterns in the Numidian site of Althiburos (2012)
sources.note: Primary archaeobiological study, Quaternary International 275, pp. 84 to 96. Publisher indexed abstract and introduction read in full; direct page returned access error. Early Numidian phases tenth/ninth to early seventh centuries BCE; crop and mammal lists plus dung microremains. Public text does not extrapolate modern ethnographic practices or assert toilets identified.

sources.title: Nacéra Sahir and Ouerdia Yermeche, Les recherches en onomastique libyco-berbère (2022)
sources.note: Directly read section Sources épigraphiques: MSNSN = Massinissa and MKWSN = Micipsa; discussion of Dougga RIL 1 and RIL 2, the latter around 138 BCE. This is a scholarly transliteration, not an invented original-script rendering. Text distinguishes languages, personal names and inscriptions.

sources.title: British Museum, Written in stone: the Libyco-Berber scripts
sources.note: Official indexed museum article read including bilingual inscription photograph caption and discussion of alphabet variation, consonants and decipherment. Direct page fetch failed. Do not adopt its accidental description of a script as a language or its apparent BCE/CE typo concerning late Saharan texts. No museum object image visually inspected.

sources.title: Chloé Capel and the MAAT mission, Azougui: Archéologie française dans le monde
sources.note: Primary mission account hosted by the French Ministry of Culture; directly read. Programme began in 2025. Medieval settlement at least eleventh century; current qasba definitively reassigned to the modern period after 1980 to 1981 research. Do not repeat obsolete Almoravid-fortress attribution in older heritage nomination.

sources.title: Mauritanian heritage nomination, Paysage culturel d’Azougui (2001)
sources.note: Official state-party description hosted by UNESCO, directly read. Used for Sanhaja/Lamtuna/Gudala origins and dated oasis practices only. This is a tentative-list nomination, not inscription as a World Heritage Site. Its old attribution of visible fortification to Almoravids is superseded by MAAT archaeological account and not used.

sources.title: British Museum, Almoravid dynasty collection term
sources.note: Official indexed institutional record checked: 1056 to 1147, Morocco and Spain. Direct fetch failed. Used only for broad dynasty chronology/geographical power, not disputed conquest of Ghana.

sources.title: D. Robert and Maurice Picon, Classification des lampes importées sur le site de Tegdaoust (1983)
sources.note: Primary archaeological study, Revue d’Archéométrie 7, pp. 59 to 69. Page 59 directly read: urban development early tenth century, copper and iron crafts, pottery and glass imports. Its wider identification of Tegdaoust/Awdaghost is followed as conventional; mixed town not claimed exclusively Amazigh. No unverified lamp typology used.

sources.title: UNESCO, The Agdal system sustaining landscapes and livelihoods in Arganeraie (2025)
sources.note: Directly read report dated 30 September 2025. Contemporary examples of restricted harvesting, assemblies and Tanast water-clock shares. Does not securely date invention to antiquity, so no such age asserted. Its loose attribution of Neolithic Oued Beht to Amazigh people and tree-age claims are not adopted.

sources.title: UNESCO, Argan: practices and know-how concerning the argan tree (2014)
sources.note: Official full indexed description read; direct returned JavaScript challenge. Contemporary craft process, family teaching and wedding gifts; no medical efficacy or medieval unchanged custom inferred.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Tent collected at Tiidrine in 1983
sources.note: Official full indexed specimen record read; direct access failed. Goat hair panels, sewing, reinforcements, repairs and spare patches/yarn. Collection date 1983, not manufacture date. Culture catalogue Amazigh/Berber; geography Tiidrine, Gorges du Todra region, Morocco.

sources.title: UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning, Amazigh-language literacy programme for argan cooperatives (2015)
sources.note: Directly read report updated 3 September 2015: programme launched December 2008; curriculum, mother-tongue DVDs, harvest schedule adjustments. Dated case study, not a claim of current enrolment or unchanged operation.

sources.title: Fatima Agnaou, L’amazighe dans l’enseignement scolaire au Maroc (IRCAM, 2021)
sources.note: Direct full primary institutional PDF read. Exact title, transliteration and French gloss at printed p. 120, PDF human p. 131 (zero 130): ⴰⵣⵓⵍ ⴰ ⵉⵎⵥⵢⴰⵏⵏ ! [azul a imẓyann !] « Salut les petits ». English translation supplied as Hello, little ones. Describes a 2007 preschool booklet for ages four to six. This is a modern Moroccan written sample, not medieval Sanhaja or every Amazigh variety. Screenshot returned cache error; readable Unicode PDF text and official indexed witness agree.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Separate ancient contextual narrative; do not associate with berbers-900 or berber-tribes.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Decoded broad Maghreb polygon, roughly 9.859 west to 18.805 east and 28.382 to 37.282 north. Not a demonstrated ethnic boundary.
batchIdentityNotes.scope: Archaeological sites illustrate local societies within the broad label, not proof that every site spoke the same Amazigh language or shared a government. Oued Beht is explicitly earlier background; Dougga writing explicitly later Numidian evidence. Kach Kouch and Althiburos supply evidence within the imported interval.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: MSNSN = Massinissa, scholarly transliteration documented in CRASC source. No original glyphs invented. The 138 BCE dedication is centuries later than this map record.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Associate two broad medieval cultural map labels in a phased regional narrative; keep ancient berbers separate.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Both polygons span much of the western Sahara and southern Morocco; approximately 17.433 west to 1.179 west/0.517 east, 13.3 to 32.45 north. They are not verified ethnic frontiers, kingdoms or modern sovereignty claims.
batchIdentityNotes.scope: Sanhaja and Almoravid origins plus Azougui/Tegdaoust provide medieval regional contexts. Later Moroccan Amazigh examples are explicitly dated and not claimed representative of every medieval Saharan population. Modern Western Sahara sovereignty is not inferred from the imported geometry.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Original modern Tifinagh title and transliteration from primary IRCAM publication; no claim that medieval western Saharan communities used this standardized spelling.
batchIdentityNotes.archaeologicalCorrection: MAAT account supersedes old UNESCO tentative nomination attribution of Azougui qasba to Almoravids. Public text makes the later date clear.
